title: Subscription tracker: dates, decisions and proof
dek: Track renewal charges and cancellation cutoffs separately, record the billing channel, and keep cancelled rows until you have checked the outcome.
metaDescription: Build a subscription tracker with billing dates, cancellation cutoffs, account owners and confirmation records so a planned cancellation becomes action.

paragraphs: A useful subscription tracker records the service, charge, billing cycle, next charge date, actual cancellation cutoff, billing channel and your next decision. Keep 'plan to cancel' separate from 'cancellation confirmed.' A renewal date is not automatically the last safe day to act.

The problem is rarely remembering that streaming costs money. It is finding out that an annual plan renews tomorrow, or discovering that the account is managed through an app store rather than the service's website. This guide organizes subscriptions you already know about. For discovery, use [how to find every subscription](/guides/how-to-find-every-subscription-you-are-paying-for).

body.heading: Keep these facts together
rows: That an unfamiliar merchant is definitely this service
That the advertised monthly equivalent is the charge
That last year's date still applies
That renewal day is early enough
Direct, app store or other intermediary; account owner
That deleting the app ends billing
Keep, review, requested cancellation, confirmed, checked
That deciding to cancel has stopped payment

body.heading: Set up the next action, not just the row
items: Verify the billing channel and next charge in the actual account.
Read the cancellation terms and record any cutoff separately.
Enter the full upcoming charge even if you also calculate a monthly equivalent.
Choose keep, review or cancel, and assign an action date before the cutoff.
Set a reminder where you will see it and confirm it was saved.
Record who will act if the service is shared.
After cancellation, save the confirmation and check the next relevant statement.

body.heading: Invented example: two dates prevent one mistake
paragraphs: A fictional annual learning app shows a $96 charge on December 10. Its account terms specify that cancellation must be completed by December 8. The tracker therefore records December 10 as the charge date, December 8 as the cutoff, and December 3 as this household's action date. December 3 is a chosen buffer, not a rule for all subscriptions.

The action owner opens the correct billing account on December 3, cancels and saves the confirmation. The row changes to 'confirmed; access ends December 10.' It remains in an archive pending a charge check. If the provider's terms are unclear, the next action is to ask for clarification, not invent a cutoff from the previous charge.

body.heading: Make the review window reach the next review
paragraphs: If you review monthly, looking ahead only two weeks leaves a gap. Review through your next scheduled review plus a practical buffer, or use more frequent reviews with verified individual reminders. The right buffer depends on the service's terms and the time you need to act.

Add trials on the day you start them, including the conversion price, trial end and cancellation instructions. The [FTC subscription guidance](https://consumer.ftc.gov/articles/getting-and-out-free-trials-auto-renewals-and-negative-option-subscriptions) advises checking terms, using reminders and retaining cancellation evidence. Do not assume that every trial can be cancelled by the same method or at the same time.

An active subscription belongs once in your overall recurring-payment total. Keep detailed decision notes here and the payment in your [monthly bills list](/guides/monthly-bills-list), without adding both records together. For shared plans, track the full provider charge and expected contributions separately.

body.heading: Keep evidence when a service ends
paragraphs: Do not delete a row as soon as you press cancel. Record the request date, confirmation reference, stated access end and where the evidence is stored. Check whether the next charge stopped or a promised refund arrived. Archive the record once the outcome is understood, retaining it as long as a dispute or other relevant need remains.

If you are charged after cancelling, contact the provider through its official channel with the evidence. Contact the payment provider promptly if the charge is unauthorized or the dispute is unresolved; deadlines depend on the payment and situation. Replacing a card or stopping a payment is not the same as ending a contract.

Store account-owner names and management links, not passwords or card security codes. If the tracker is shared, remove unrelated personal services before sending it. A practical list should not become a shared credential file.

items.q: Is the renewal date the cancellation deadline?
items.a: Not necessarily. The provider may require action earlier or through a particular channel. Record the next charge and actual cutoff as separate fields, then set your own action date before the cutoff. Confirm uncertain terms rather than treating a reminder as proof you can still cancel.

Move them to an archive rather than deleting the evidence. Keep the request, confirmation and next charge check together. If cancellation failed or the next payment still appears, that record helps explain the problem and gives you something specific to send when following up.

items.q: Can paper work as a subscription tracker?
items.a: Yes. The format matters less than accurate dates, a named action owner and reminders outside a page you may not open. Paper can hold the record; a calendar can carry the action date. Update both when the service changes its price or terms.

worksheet.title: Subscription renewal and cancellation record
worksheet.prompt: Separate the payment date from the action deadline and preserve the outcome.

research.intent: Maintain verified renewal and cancellation records after subscriptions have been found.

limitations: No claim of universal cancellation rights or cutoffs.
Provider-specific terms must be checked by the reader.
